e-21675.problem:
Given the system of differential equations, determine whether the system is almost linear at the equilibrium point $\mathbf{x}^\ast= [0, \: 0]^T.$

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-{y}^{2}(t)+1-{e}^{x(t)} \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-{x}^{2}(t)+1-{e}^{y(t)}\end{aligned}
$$
e-21675.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
\mathbf{x}' = \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x})
$$

where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094758/assets/58d027aeb94fddf42231a86a73de4be306fa6ea22ea7767dbe8a461e91a6f446.png) and 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094758/assets/bb9297479f2149dfca76e02fb9e314205063fd3a3f967d70eee24235970206b1.png)

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094758/assets/6ea02cc0d71b67f061adb67ee344cc5474b71e1e34db122b942d2e0ed1531ae8.png)

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{y}^{2}+1-{e}^{x})=-{e}^{x},\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{y}^{2}+1-{e}^{x})=-2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{x}^{2}+1-{e}^{y})=-2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{x}^{2}+1-{e}^{y})=-{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094758/assets/8f1e68dd09715b24f0de6c79fdf07af6e9810741e1a6065637db5301cd86ebe0.png)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094758/assets/ef4a060144a80ac9ecb94a71c407d1537283ecc217ac26ab053e9b8d2fad73e9.png) to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(0,0) & =|\begin{aligned}-{e}^{0} & -2(0) \\ -2(0) & -{e}^{0}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-1)(-1)-(0)(0) \\  & =1 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is not zero, our system is $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{almost linear}}$ at $\mathbf{x}^\ast.$
